inline.s: Excerpted from
A Detailed Commentary on the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch

[The Chan practitioner Zhihuang, when he first visited the Fifth Patriarch, claimed that he had already attained right absorption, and sat in a thatched hut for twenty years. The Master’s disciple Xuance, wandering in quest of the Way, came to the region north of the Yellow River. Hearing of Zhihuang’s renown, he called at the hut and asked: What are you doing here? Zhihuang said: Entering samādhi.]

The Chan practitioner Zhihuang, when he first visited the Fifth Patriarch Hongren, thought he had already attained samādhi (right absorption), and sat alone in a thatched hut for as long as twenty years. Xuance, a disciple of the Sixth Patriarch, came wandering in quest of the Way to the region north of the Yellow River. Hearing the renown of Chan Master Zhihuang for his skill in Chan meditation, he called at the thatched hut and asked: What are you doing here? Zhihuang replied: Entering samādhi.

[Right absorption] the meditation in which the thinking mind is wholly stilled and conditioned reflections cease together, also called samādhi. [Wandering in quest of the Way] traveling about to monasteries everywhere to study and inquire about the Way. [North of the Yellow River] generally refers to the region north of the Yellow River. [Call at] to go to, to arrive at; for example, to pay a visit.

[Xuance said: You say you are entering samādhi — do you enter it with mind, or without mind? If you enter without mind, then all insentient things, the grass, trees, tiles, and stones, should also attain samādhi; if you enter with mind, then all sentient beings that possess consciousness should also attain samādhi.]

Xuance said: You say you are entering samādhi — do you enter it with mind, or without mind? If you enter without mind, then all insentient things, the grass, trees, tiles, and stones, being all without mind, should all attain samādhi; if you enter with mind, then all sentient beings, having mind, should all attain samādhi.
[Possessing consciousness] those that contain mind-consciousness, that is, sentient beings.

[Zhihuang said: When I am truly entering samādhi, I do not see any mind that either has or lacks mind. Xuance said: If you do not see any mind that has or lacks mind, this is constant samādhi — how can there be entering or leaving? If there is entering and leaving, it is not the great samādhi. Zhihuang had no reply.]

Zhihuang said: When I am truly entering samādhi, I do not see whether there is mind or no mind. Xuance said: Since you do not see “mind or no mind,” this is constant samādhi — at no time are you not in samādhi, so how can there be any leaving or entering of samādhi? (This refers to Zhihuang’s earlier words, “Entering samādhi.”) If samādhi has leaving and entering, it is not the great samādhi. Zhihuang had no words with which to reply.

[After a long silence, he asked: Whom do you succeed as teacher? Xuance said: My teacher is the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi. Zhihuang said: What does the Sixth Patriarch regard as Chan meditation? Xuance said: What my teacher teaches is this: the nature is wondrously clear and perfectly quiescent, its essence and function in suchness; the five skandhas are fundamentally empty, the six sense-objects are not existent, with no leaving and no entering, no samādhi and no confusion. The nature of Chan is without abiding, so it is apart from abiding in the quiescence of Chan; the nature of Chan is without arising, so it is apart from arising the thought of Chan. The mind is like empty space, yet without the measure of empty space.]

After a long silence, Zhihuang asked: May I ask who your teacher is? Xuance said: My teacher is the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi. Zhihuang said: Then what does the Sixth Patriarch regard as Chan meditation? Xuance said: What my teacher teaches is this: the fundamental nature is wondrously clear and perfectly quiescent, its essence and function in suchness; the five skandhas (the five aggregates, referring to body and mind) are fundamentally empty, the six sense-objects (referring to the inner and outer realms) are not existent, with no leaving and no entering, no samādhi and no confusion. The nature of Chan is without abiding, so it does not abide in the quiescence of Chan; the nature of Chan is without arising, so it does not give rise to the thought of Chan. The mind is like empty space, yet it has no thought of empty space (it does not cling to the view of emptiness).
This is to say: not being deluded before objects, remaining unmoved in suchness, and dissolving both existence and non-existence — this is true samādhi.

[Suchness] in accord with true suchness. This is the realm of self-nature that is equal and non-dual, free from inverted discrimination. [True suchness] “True” means the true mark; “suchness” means just so; the true mark being just so is called “true suchness,” that is, the true reality of all dharmas. [True reality of all dharmas] See in detail
The True Reality of All Dharmas

[When Zhihuang heard this teaching, he came straight away to pay his respects to the Master. The Master asked: Where have you come from, worthy one? Zhihuang recounted in full the preceding events. The Master said: It is truly as has been said. You need only make your mind like empty space, yet without clinging to the view of emptiness; let its functioning be unobstructed, without mind in movement or stillness, forgetting the feelings of ordinary and holy, with both the perceiving and the perceived dissolved, so that nature and mark are in suchness — and there will be no time when you are not in samādhi.]

When Zhihuang heard this teaching, he came straight away to pay his respects to the Sixth Patriarch. The Sixth Patriarch asked: What brings you here, worthy one? Zhihuang recounted in full his meeting with Xuance. The Sixth Patriarch said: The principle of samādhi is truly as Xuance said. You need only make your mind like empty space, yet without clinging to emptiness; let its functioning be unobstructed, without mind in movement or stillness, giving rise neither to the view of the ordinary nor to the view of the holy (forgetting the feelings of ordinary and holy), with both the perceiving and the perceived dissolved, so that principle and marks interpenetrate without obstruction — and naturally there is no time when you are not in samādhi.

[Perceiving and perceived] That which acts of itself is called “the perceiving” (néng); that which is acted upon is called “the perceived” (suǒ). For example, when the six sense-organs meet the six sense-objects, the six sense-organs are the perceiving condition, and the six sense-objects are the perceived condition.
On the great samādhi of no leaving and no entering, Mr. Wang Xianglu, in his Process of Realizing the Essence and Putting It into Function, says:

“When objects come, pay them no heed and give rise to no thought, yet do not cut them off entirely — this is samādhi in stillness; not being deluded before objects, yet still responding to them, moving without moving — this is samādhi in movement; when movement and stillness become one suchness, with nothing to affirm and nothing to deny, this is the great samādhi.”
The sutra itself says:

“What is called Chan meditation? Outwardly to be free of marks is Chan; inwardly not to be disturbed is meditation. If outwardly one clings to marks, the mind within is disturbed; if outwardly one is free of marks, the mind is not disturbed. The fundamental nature is of itself pure and of itself settled; only because one sees objects and thinks about them does it become disturbed. If, seeing the various objects, the mind is not disturbed, this is true samādhi.”

[Thereupon Zhihuang had a great awakening, and the mind of attainment he had gained in twenty years vanished without a trace. That night, the scholars and commoners of the north of the Yellow River heard a voice in the sky saying: Chan Master Zhihuang has attained the Way today! Later Zhihuang took his leave with due ceremony, returned to the north of the Yellow River, and taught and transformed the four assemblies.]

Thereupon Zhihuang had a great awakening, and the mind of attainment he had gained through twenty years of sitting in samādhi vanished without a trace. That night, the people of the north of the Yellow River all heard a voice in the sky saying (the praise of heavenly beings): Chan Master Zhihuang has attained the Way today! Later Zhihuang took his leave of the Sixth Patriarch with due ceremony, returned to the north of the Yellow River, and taught and transformed the four assemblies of monks and laypeople.

A clear-sighted teacher removes adhesions and unties bonds: for many years Zhihuang had still clung to attaining samādhi and entering samādhi; now that the adhesion and bondage were removed, the sea is wide and the sky is vast — there is no time not in samādhi.
